docs.title: Compression formats
docs.text:
PCSX.Compression encodes and decodes LZSS-family formats that are described from Lua. There are no built-in formats: every codec comes from a description. The description is a grammar, because the variation between these formats is in the productions: how a stream terminates, how its window works, which byte fills a reference below the start of the output, and which token encodings are carved out as escapes.

PCSX.Compression.schema(description) validates the description and returns a codec object. It raises an error if the description is invalid.

local lz = PCSX.Compression.schema {
    name = 'example',
    control = { unit = 1, perGroup = 8, lsbFirst = true, oneMeans = 'literal' },
    window  = { base = 'relative', maxDist = 0x0fff, fillByte = 0, overlap = true },
    emit    = { ringSize = 4096 },
    productions = {
        -- fill: a length nibble of 0xf is the escape
        { bytes = 2,
          guards = { { at = { 1, 0xf0, -4 }, eq = 0x0f } },
          fill = { run = { at = { 1, 0x0f }, bias = 3 }, value = { at = { 0, 0xff } } } },
        -- match: 12-bit distance, 4-bit length
        { bytes = 2,
          match = { len = { at = { 1, 0xf0, -4 }, bias = 3 },
                    dist = { at = { { 0, 0xff, 0 }, { 1, 0x0f, 8 } } } } },
    },
}

local plain = lz:decode(compressed, sizeOut)
local packed = lz:encode(plain)

docs.title: The description
docs.text:
The stream is a sequence of groups. Each group starts with a control unit, whose bits say, item by item, whether the next item is a literal byte (or unit) or a token.

  • name: a string used in diagnostics.
  • control:
    • unit: size of a control unit in bytes, 1 or 2. Only the first byte of a 2-byte unit is read. Default 1.
    • perGroup: how many items one unit describes, 1 to 8. Default 8.
    • lsbFirst: whether bit 0 is consumed first, otherwise bit 7. Default true.
    • oneMeans: 'literal' (default) means a set bit is a literal, 'token' means a set bit selects a production.
    • reverseBits: bit-reverse each control byte before use.
  • window:
    • base: how a distance becomes a source position. 'relative' (default) is the output position minus the distance. 'absolute' is the distance minus start. 'windowEnd' is the output position minus maxDist, minus 1, plus the distance, minus start, and requires maxDist.
    • start, maxDist, distBias: the window start, the window size, and a bias added to every decoded distance. Default 0.
    • fillByte: the byte a reference below the start of the output yields. Default 0.
    • overlap: whether a match may overlap its own output. Default true.
  • emit: constraints for the encoder only, kept apart from what the decoder accepts:
    • ringSize: size of the runtime window ring, which caps the distances the encoder emits. 0 means no cap.
    • allowNegative: whether the encoder may reference before the start of the output.
    • terminator: whether the encoder appends the stop production.
  • productions: up to 4. Each one is tried in order, and the first whose guards all pass wins, so a guarded production shadows part of the encoding space of an unguarded one after it. That is how these formats carve escapes out of a fixed token width. A production has:
    • bytes: how many bytes the token takes, 1 to 4, including the ones the guards read.
    • guards: up to 2 conditions, each { at = ..., eq = n } or { at = ..., ne = n }, tested against the raw value before any bias.
    • exactly one of match = { len = field, dist = field }, fill = { run = field, value = field }, or stop = true. A match copies len bytes from the source position. A fill writes run copies of value. A stop ends the stream, and its presence makes the stream run until that token, rather than until the output size.

A field is { at = term, bias = n }, where at is either one term or a list of up to three, and the terms are or'ed together before the bias is added. A term is { byte, mask, shift }: byte byte of the token, masked, then shifted left by shift, or right if it's negative. shift defaults to 0.

docs.title: The codec
docs.text:
• lz:decode(input, outSize) returns the plain string, a statistics table, and how many input bytes were consumed. input is a string or a Slice, and outSize is what the container says the payload decodes to; a schema with a stop production still takes it as a safety cap. It raises an error with the reason, such as running out of input or no production matching a token.
  • lz:encode(input[, lazy]) returns the compressed string. A lazy parse is used when lazy is true, a greedy one otherwise. The encoder only supports 'relative' windows, and checks its candidate tokens against the decoder's own production selector, so it never emits an encoding a guard has stolen.
  • lz:probe(input, outSize) returns true and a table { bytes, consumed, stats } if the input plausibly decodes under the schema, or false and the reason. It doesn't raise errors, so it can be swept across a buffer looking for payloads.

The statistics table has match, fill, literal (token counts), overlapping (matches whose distance is shorter than their length), negativeRefs (references before the start of the output), and, when there was a token of the kind, distMin, distMax, lenMin, lenMax, runMin, runMax. They describe what the original encoder emitted, which is the best evidence of what the target's own decoder tolerates.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
The Lua code can listen for events broadcasted from within the emulator. The following function is available to register a callback to be called when certain events happen:

PCSX.Events.createEventListener(eventName, callback)

Important: the return value of this function will be an object that represents the listener itself. If this object gets garbage collected, the corresponding listener will be removed. Thus it is important to store it somewhere that won't get garbage collected right away. The listener object has a :remove method to stop the listener before its garbage collection time.

The callback function will be called from an unsecured environment, and it is advised to delegate anything complex or risky enough to PCSX.nextTick.

The eventName argument is a string that can have the following values:

  • Quitting: The emulator is about to quit. The callback will be called with an empty table. This is where you'd need to close libuv objects held by Lua through luv in order to allow the emulator to quit gracefully. Otherwise you may soft lock the application where it'll wait for libuv objects to close.
  • IsoMounted: A new ISO file has been mounted into the virtual CDRom drive. The callback will be called with an empty table.
  • GPU::Vsync: The emulated GPU has just completed a vertical blanking interval. The callback will be called with an empty table.
  • ExecutionFlow::ShellReached: The emulation execution has reached the beginning of the BIOS' shell. The callback will be called with an empty table. This is the moment where the kernel is properly set up and ready to execute any arbitrary binary. The emulator may use this event to side load binaries, or signal gdb that the kernel is ready.
  • ExecutionFlow::Run: The emulator resumed execution. The callback will be called with an empty table. This event will fire when calling PCSX.resumeEmulator(), when the user presses Start, or other potential interactions.
  • ExecutionFlow::Pause: The emulator paused execution. The callback will be called with a table that contains a boolean named exception, indicating if the pause is the result of an execution exception within the emulated CPU. This event will fire on breakpoints too, so if breakpoints have Lua callbacks attached on them, they will be executed too.
  • ExecutionFlow::Reset: The emulator is resetting the emulated machine. The callback will be called with a table that contains a boolean named hard, indicating if the reset is a hard reset or a soft reset. This event will fire when calling PCSX.softResetEmulator() or PCSX.hardResetEmulator(), when the user presses Reset, or other potential interactions.
  • ExecutionFlow::SaveStateLoaded: The emulator just loaded a savestate. The callback will be called with an empty table. This event will fire when calling PCSX.loadSaveState(), when the user loads a savestate, or other potential interactions. This is useful to listen to in case some internal state needs to be reset within the Lua logic.
  • GUI::JumpToPC: The UI is being asked to move the assembly view cursor to the specified address. The callback will be called with a table that contains a number named pc, indicating the address to jump to.
  • GUI::JumpToMemory: The UI is being asked to move the memory view cursor to the specified address. The callback will be called with a table that contains a number named address, indicating the address to jump to, and size, indicating the number of bytes to highlight.
  • Keyboard: The emulator is dispatching keyboard events. The callback will be called with a table containing four numbers: key, scancode, action, and mods. key is the SDL keycode, scancode the SDL scancode, action is 1 for a key press and 0 for a release, and mods holds the SDL modifier flags. SDL scancodes use the USB HID keyboard usage numbers. Key repeats arrive as further presses.
  • Memory::SetLuts: The emulator has updated the memory LUTs. The callback will be called with an empty table.

docs.title: Introduction & Rationale
docs.text:
The PlayStation's parallel port, also known as EXP1, maps the cartridge connected to it at 0x1f000000 to 0x1f7fffff. PCSX-Redux emulates one cartridge natively, the PIO cart found under Configuration > PIO Cartridge. Anything else, be it a development board, a USB adapter, or a cheat device behaving slightly differently, can be emulated from Lua, without touching the emulator's code, by combining the memory LUTs and the unmapped memory callbacks described in Memory and registers.

The short version: a memory access whose page has no entry in the LUTs, and which isn't claimed by the emulator itself, is forwarded to the global Lua functions UnknownMemoryRead and UnknownMemoryWrite. A cart in Lua makes sure its pages have no LUT entry, and then answers these callbacks.

docs.title: How an access reaches Lua
docs.text:
For each read or write, the CPU looks up the 64kB page of the address, address >> 16, in the read or write LUT. In order:

  • If the LUT entry is not nil, the access goes straight to the memory it points to, and Lua never sees it.
  • Pages 0x1f80, 0x9f80 and 0xbf80, the scratchpad and the hardware registers, are always handled by the emulator.
  • If the native PIO cart is connected, all of 0x1f000000 to 0x1f7fffff goes to it. So the native PIO cart has to be disconnected for a Lua cart to work.
  • Otherwise, the access is forwarded to Lua.

Each page is reachable through three addresses, one per memory segment: 0x1f00 for KUSEG, 0x9f00 for KSEG0, and 0xbf00 for KSEG1. The LUTs have one entry for each, so a cart needs to handle all three.

docs.title: Claiming a range
docs.text:
When the native PIO cart is disconnected, the EXP1 pages have no LUT entry, and every access already reaches Lua. However, another script may have mapped them, so a cart should clear the pages it wants to trap explicitly, through the pointers returned by PCSX.getReadLUT() and PCSX.getWriteLUT():

local pages = { 0x1f00, 0x9f00, 0xbf00 }

local function claim()
    local readLUT = PCSX.getReadLUT()
    local writeLUT = PCSX.getWriteLUT()
    if readLUT == nil or writeLUT == nil then return end
    for _, page in ipairs(pages) do
        readLUT[page] = nil
        writeLUT[page] = nil
    end
end

The emulator signals the Memory::SetLuts event when it rebuilds its memory LUTs, so a cart should listen to it and claim its pages again, keeping the listener object alive as explained in Events.

A cart which holds actual memory, such as a ROM, can do the opposite for its read pages: point them to a buffer allocated with ffi.new, and reads will then be served at full speed without going through Lua. The buffer must stay referenced from Lua for as long as the LUT points to it, otherwise the garbage collector will free memory the emulated CPU is still reading. Writes to a ROM or a flash chip usually still need to go through Lua, so their write pages stay nil.

docs.title: The callbacks
docs.text:
function UnknownMemoryRead(address, size) end
function UnknownMemoryWrite(address, size, value) end
  • address is the full address used by the CPU, including its segment: a read from KSEG1 arrives as 0xbf000100, not 0x1f000100. Mask it with bit.band(address, 0x1fffffff) to get the physical address.
  • size is 1, 2 or 4, depending on the instruction.
  • For a read, returning a number makes it the value read by the CPU. It should fit in size bytes. Returning nothing at all leaves the read unhandled, and the emulator carries on as if the function didn't exist, which usually means the CPU reads 0xff, 0xffff or 0xffffffff. Careful: returning nil explicitly still counts as a value, and the CPU will read 0.
  • For a write, returning true marks it as handled. Anything else leaves it unhandled.
  • If either function raises an error, the error is printed in the console, the access is left unhandled, and the emulator removes the global by setting it to nil. A buggy cart therefore disconnects itself on its first error.

These are two global names, so only one script at a time can own them. A cart which only handles its own addresses should keep the previous functions and forward everything else to them, as the example below does.

docs.title: Disconnecting
docs.text: A cart which can be unplugged needs to undo what it did when it was connected: remove its Memory::SetLuts listener, put back the LUT entries it saved when connecting, and restore the previous UnknownMemoryRead and UnknownMemoryWrite functions. A cart which pointed LUT entries to its own buffers has to remove these before letting the buffers go.

docs.title: Packaging
docs.text:
A cart made of several files is easiest to distribute as a zip file. When a zip file is loaded, its autoexec.lua file, if present, is executed, and Support.extra.dofile will find the other Lua files of the archive. There are several ways to load it:

  • From the command line, using the -archive flag, as in pcsx-redux -archive mycart.zip.
  • From the File menu, using Add Lua archive.
  • By dragging and dropping the zip file onto the main window.
  • From Lua, using Support.extra.addArchive(filename).

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
This cart exposes a single 32-bit status register at 0x1f000100. Each read returns a counter which increments on every access, and writing to it sets the counter. All the other addresses are forwarded to whatever was handling them before.

CounterCart = {
    register = 0x1f000100,
    counter = 0,
    pages = { 0x1f00, 0x9f00, 0xbf00 },
    connected = false,
}

function CounterCart.claim()
    local readLUT = PCSX.getReadLUT()
    local writeLUT = PCSX.getWriteLUT()
    if readLUT == nil or writeLUT == nil then return end
    for _, page in ipairs(CounterCart.pages) do
        readLUT[page] = nil
        writeLUT[page] = nil
    end
end

function CounterCart.read(address, size)
    if bit.band(address, 0x1fffffff) == CounterCart.register then
        CounterCart.counter = (CounterCart.counter + 1) % 0x100000000
        return CounterCart.counter
    end
    if CounterCart.previousRead then return CounterCart.previousRead(address, size) end
end

function CounterCart.write(address, size, value)
    if bit.band(address, 0x1fffffff) == CounterCart.register then
        CounterCart.counter = value
        return true
    end
    if CounterCart.previousWrite then return CounterCart.previousWrite(address, size, value) end
    return false
end

function CounterCart.connect()
    if CounterCart.connected then return end
    local readLUT = PCSX.getReadLUT()
    local writeLUT = PCSX.getWriteLUT()
    CounterCart.saved = {}
    for _, page in ipairs(CounterCart.pages) do
        CounterCart.saved[page] = { readLUT[page], writeLUT[page] }
    end
    CounterCart.previousRead = UnknownMemoryRead
    CounterCart.previousWrite = UnknownMemoryWrite
    UnknownMemoryRead = CounterCart.read
    UnknownMemoryWrite = CounterCart.write
    CounterCart.claim()
    CounterCart.listener = PCSX.Events.createEventListener('Memory::SetLuts', CounterCart.claim)
    CounterCart.connected = true
end

function CounterCart.disconnect()
    if not CounterCart.connected then return end
    CounterCart.listener:remove()
    CounterCart.listener = nil
    local readLUT = PCSX.getReadLUT()
    local writeLUT = PCSX.getWriteLUT()
    for page, pointers in pairs(CounterCart.saved) do
        readLUT[page] = pointers[1]
        writeLUT[page] = pointers[2]
    end
    UnknownMemoryRead = CounterCart.previousRead
    UnknownMemoryWrite = CounterCart.previousWrite
    CounterCart.connected = false
end

CounterCart.connect()

Saved as autoexec.lua in a zip file and loaded with -archive, the cart is connected before the emulated machine starts. On the PlayStation side, reading the register is a plain load:

volatile uint32_t *counter = (volatile uint32_t *)0xbf000100;
uint32_t first = *counter;  // 1
uint32_t second = *counter; // 2
*counter = 41;
uint32_t third = *counter;  // 42

A byte or halfword access to the same address goes through the same function, with size set to 1 or 2. The value returned should fit in that size.

docs.title: Complete examples
docs.text:
John Baumann's lua-pio-cart emulates a cheat cartridge with its PAL and SST29EE020 flash chip using these same mechanisms, with its ROM mapped into the read LUT and its control registers trapped through the callbacks. It is packaged as a zip file and is a good starting point for a more complex cart.

redux-ch376-cart emulates a CH376 USB host controller in parallel mode at 0x1f400000, with a USB boot keyboard attached that follows the PC keyboard through the Keyboard event. It traps both of its registers through the callbacks and maps no memory.

docs.title: Introduction & Rationale
docs.text:
While the normal Lua io API is loaded, there's a more powerful API that's more tightly integrated with the rest of the PCSX-Redux File handling code. It's an abstraction class that allows seamless manipulation of various objects using a common API.

The File objects have different properties depending on how they are created and their intention. But generally speaking, the following rules apply:

  • Files are reference counted. They will be deleted when the reference count reaches zero. The Lua garbage collector will only decrease the reference count.
  • Whenever possible, writes are deferred to an asynchronous thread, making writes return basically instantly. This speed up comes at the trade off of data integrity, which means writes aren't guaranteed to be flushed to the disk yet when the function returns. Data will always have integrity internally within PCSX-Redux however, and when exiting normally, all data will be flushed to the disk.
  • Some File objects can be cached. When caching, reads and writes will be done transparently, and the cache will be used instead of the actual file. This will make reads return basically instantly too.
  • The Read and Write APIs can haul LuaBuffer objects. These are Lua objects that can be used to read and write data to the file. You can construct one using the Support.NewLuaBuffer(size) function. They can be cast to strings, and can be used as a table for reading and writing bytes off of it, in a 0-based fashion. The length operator will return the size of the buffer. The methods :maxsize() and :resize(size) are available. They also have a .pbSlice property that implicitly converts them to a Lua-Protobuf's pb.slice, which can then be passed to pb.decode.
  • The Read and Write APIs can also function using Lua-Protobuf's buffers and slices respectively.
  • If the file isn't closed when the file object is destroyed, it'll be closed then, but letting the garbage collector do the closing is not recommended. This is because the garbage collector will only run when the memory pressure is high enough, and the file handle will be held for a long time.
  • When using streamed functions, unlike POSIX files handles, there's two distinct seeking pointers: one for reading and one for writing.

docs.title: Common API for all File objects
docs.text:
All File objects have the following API attached to them as methods:

Closes and frees any associated resources. Better to call this manually than letting the garbage collector do it: 

:close()

Reads from the File object and advances the read pointer accordingly. The return value depends on the variant used. 

:read(size)            -- returns a LuaBuffer
:read(ptr, size)       -- returns the number of bytes read, ptr has to be a cdata of pointer type
:read(buffer)          -- returns the number of bytes read, and adjusts the buffer's size
:read(pb_buffer, size) -- returns the number of bytes read, while appending to the pb_buffer's existing data
:gets()                -- returns a string, up to the next newline character

Reads from the File object at the specified position. No pointers are modified. The return value depends on the variant used, just like the non-At variants above. 

:readAt(size, pos)
:readAt(ptr, size, pos)
:readAt(buffer, pos)
:readAt(pb_buffer, size, pos)

Writes to the File object. The non-At variants will advances the write pointer accordingly. The At variants will not modify the write pointer, and simply write at the requested location. Returns the number of bytes written. The string variants will in fact take any object that can be transformed to a string using tostring(). 

:write(string)
:write(buffer)
:write(slice)
:write(pb_slice)
:write(ptr, size)
:writeAt(string, pos)
:writeAt(buffer, pos)
:writeAt(slice, pos)
:writeAt(pb_slice, pos)
:writeAt(ptr, size, pos)

Note that in this context, pb_slice and pb_buffer refer to Lua-Protobuf's pb.slice and pb.buffer objects respectively.

Some APIs may return a Slice object, which is an opaque buffer coming from C++. The write and writeAt methods can take a Slice. It is possible to write a slice to a file in a zero-copy manner, which will be more efficient:

:writeMoveSlice(slice)
:writeAtMoveSlice(slice, pos)

After which, the slice will be consumed and not reusable. The Slice object is convertible to a string using tostring(), and also has, among others, the members data, which is a const void*, and size. Once consumed by the MoveSlice variants, the size of a slice will go down to zero.

Finally, it is possible to convert a Slice object to a pb.slice one using the Support.sliceToPBSlice function. However, the same caveats as for normal pb.slice objects apply: it is fragile, and will be invalidated if the underlying Slice is moved or destroyed, so it is recommended to use it as a temporary object, such as an argument to pb.decode. Still, it is a much faster alternative to calling tostring() which will make a copy of the underlying slice.

The following methods manipulate the read and write pointers. All of them return their corresponding pointer. The wheel argument can be of the values 'SEEK_SET', 'SEEK_CUR', and 'SEEK_END', and will default to 'SEEK_SET'. 

:rSeek(pos[, wheel])
:rTell()
:wSeek(pos[, wheel])
:wTell()

These will query the corresponding File object. 

:size()      -- Returns the size in bytes, if possible. If the file is not seekable, will throw an error.
:seekable()  -- Returns true if the file is seekable.
:writable()  -- Returns true if the file is writable.
:eof()       -- Returns true if the read pointer is at the end of file.
:failed()    -- Returns true if the file failed in some ways. The File object is defunct if this is true.
:cacheable() -- Returns true if the file is cacheable.
:caching()   -- Returns true if caching is in progress or completed.
:cacheProgress() -- Returns a value between 0 and 1 indicating the progress of the caching operation.

If applicable, this will start caching the corresponding file in memory. 

:startCaching()

Same as above, but will suspend the current coroutine until the caching is done. Cannot be used with the main thread. 

:startCachingAndWait()

Duplicates the File object. This will re-open the file, and possibly duplicate all ressources associated with it. 

:dup()

Creates a read-only view of the file starting at the specified position, spanning the specified length. The view will be a new File object, and will be a view of the same underlying file. The default values of start and length are 0 and -1 respectively, which will effectively create a view of the entire file. The view may have less features than the underlying file, but will always be seekable, and keep its seeking position independent of the underlying file. The view will hold a reference to the underlying file. 

:subFile([start[, length]])

In addition to the above methods, the File API has these helpers, that'll read or write binary values off their corresponding stream position for the non-At variants, or at the indicated position for the At variants. All the values will be read or stored in Little Endian, regardless of the host's endianness. 

:readU8(), :readU16(), :readU32(), :readU64(),
:readI8(), :readI16(), :readI32(), :readI64(),
:readU8At(pos), :readU16At(pos), :readU32At(pos), :readU64At(pos),
:readI8At(pos), :readI16At(pos), :readI32At(pos), :readI64At(pos),
:writeU8(val), :writeU16(val), :writeU32(val), :writeU64(val),
:writeI8(val), :writeI16(val), :writeI32(val), :writeI64(val),
:writeU8At(val, pos), :writeU16At(val, pos), :writeU32At(val, pos), :writeU64At(val, pos),
:writeI8At(val, pos), :writeI16At(val, pos), :writeI32At(val, pos), :writeI64At(val, pos),

docs.title: Creating File objects
docs.text:
The Lua VM can create File objects in different ways: 

Support.File.open(filename[, type])
Support.File.buffer()
Support.File.buffer(ptr, size[, type])
Support.File.mem4g()
Support.File.uvFifo(address, port)
Support.File.zReader(file[, size[, raw]])

docs.title: Basic files
docs.text:
The open function will function on filesystem and network URLs, while the buffer function will generate a memory-only File object that's fully readable, writable, and seekable. The type argument of the open function will determine what happens exactly. It's a string that can have the following values:

  • READ: Opens the file for reading only. Will fail if the file does not exist. This is the default type.
  • TRUNCATE: Opens the file for reading and writing. If the file does not exist, it will be created. If it does exist, it will be truncated to 0 size.
  • CREATE: Opens the file for reading and writing. If the file does not exist, it will be created. If it does exist, it will be left untouched.
  • READWRITE: Opens the file for reading and writing. Will fail if the file does not exist.
  • DOWNLOAD_URL: Opens the file for reading only. Will immediately start downloading the file from the network. The filename argument will be treated as a URL. The curl is the backend for this feature, and its url schemes are supported. The progress of the download can be monitored with the :cacheProgress() method.
  • DOWNLOAD_URL_AND_WAIT: As above, but suspends the current coroutine until the download is done. Cannot be used with the main thread.

docs.title: Buffers
docs.text:
When calling .buffer() with no argument, this will create an empty read-write buffer. When calling it with a cdata pointer and a size, this will have the following behavior, depending on type:

  • READWRITE (or no type): The memory passed as an argument will be copied first.
  • READ: The memory passed as an argument will be referenced, and the lifespan of said memory needs to outlast the File object. The File object will be read-only.
  • ACQUIRE: It will acquire the pointer passed as an argument, and free it later using free(), meaning it needs to have been allocated using malloc() in the first place.

The .mem4g() constructor will return a sparse buffer that has a virtual 4GB span. It can be used to read and write data in the 4GB range, but will not actually allocate any memory until the data is actually written to. This is useful for doing operations that are similar to that of the PlayStation memory. The .mem4g() constructor will return a File object that's fully readable, writable, and seekable. Its size will always be 4GB. The returned object will have 3 additional methods:

  • :lowestAddress(): Returns the lowest address that has been written to.
  • :highestAddress(): Returns the highest address that has been written to.
  • :actualSize(): Returns the size of the buffer, which is the highest address minus the lowest address.

This is a useful object to use with the :subFile() method, as it will allow you to create a view of a specific range of the 4GB memory. Specifically, obj:subFile(obj:lowestAddress(), obj:actualSize()) will create a view of the entire memory that has been written to.

docs.title: Network streams
docs.text: The uvFifo function will create a File object that will read from and write to the specified TCP address and port after connecting to it. The :failed() method will return true in case of a connection failure. The address is a string, and must be a strict IP address, no hostnames allowed. The port is a number between 1 and 65535 inclusive. As the name suggests, this object is a FIFO, meaning that incoming bytes will be consumed by any read operation. The :size() method will return the number of bytes in the FIFO. Writes will be immediately sent over. There are no reception guarantees, as the other side might have disconnected at any point. The :eof() method will return true when the opposite end of the stream has been disconnected and there's no more bytes in the FIFO. In addition to the normal File API, a uvFifo has a method called :isConnecting(), which returns a boolean indicating the fifo is still connecting, meaning it's possible to verify if the fifo has successfully connected using the boolean expression not fifo:isConnecting() and not fifo:failed().

docs.title: Compressed streams
docs.text: The zReader function will create a read-only File object which decompresses the data from the specified File object. The file argument is a File object, and the size argument is an optional number that will be used to determine the size of the decompressed data. If not specified, the resulting file won't be seekable, and its :size() method won't work, but the file will be readable until :eof() returns true. The raw argument is an optional string that needs to be equal to 'RAW', and will determine whether the data is compressed using the raw deflate format, or the zlib format. Any other string means the zlib format will be used.

docs.title: Iso files
docs.text:
There is a fairly complete API for working with ISO files. Two related topics have their own pages: creating new images from scratch is covered in Building ISO images, and the patch generation mechanism behind the :savePPF() method below is covered in PPF patches.

  • PCSX.getCurrentIso() will return an Iso object representing the currently loaded ISO file by the emulator.
  • PCSX.openIso(pathOrFile) will return an Iso object opened from the specified argument, which can either be a filesystem path, or a File object.

The following methods are available on the Iso object:

:failed()       -- Returns true if the Iso file failed in some ways. The Iso object is defunct if this is true.
:createReader() -- Returns an ISOReader object off the Iso file.
:open(lba[, size[, mode]]) -- Returns a File object off the specified span of sectors.
:clearPPF()     -- Clears out all of the currently applied patches.
:savePPF()      -- Saves the currently applied patches to a PPF file named after the ISO file.
:getTN()        -- Returns the number of tracks. An image without a track table reports 1.
:getTD(track)   -- Returns the start of the track as an MSF struct with m, s and f fields, as plain numbers. Track 0 returns the position past the last track, and a single track image or an out of range track returns 00:02:00.

The :open method has some magic built-in. The size argument is optional, and if missing, the code will attempt to guess the size of the underlying file within the Iso. It will represent the size of the virtual file in bytes. The size guessing mechanism can only work on MODE2 FORM1 or FORM2 sectors, and will result in a failed File object otherwise. The mode argument is optional, and can be one of the following:

  • 'GUESS': will attempt to guess the mode of the file. This is the default.
  • 'RAW': the returned File object will read 2352 bytes per sector.
  • 'M1': the returned File object will read 2048 bytes per sector.
  • 'M2_RAW': the returned File object will read 2336 bytes per sector. This can't be guessed. This is useful for extracting STR files that require the subheaders to be present.
  • 'M2_FORM1': the returned File object will read 2048 bytes per sector.
  • 'M2_FORM2': the returned File object will read 2324 bytes per sector.

The resulting File object will cache a single full sector in memory, meaning that small sequential reads won't read the same sector over and over from the disk.

The resulting File object will be writable, which will temporarily patch the CD-Rom image file in memory. It is possible to flush the patches to a PPF file by calling the :savePPF() method of the corresponding Iso object. When writing to one of these files, the filesystem metadata information will not be updated, meaning that the size of the file on the filesystem will not change, despite it being possible to write past the end of it and overflow on the next sectors. Note that while the virtual File object will enlarge to accommodate the writes, it will not be filled with zeroes as with typical filesystem operations, but instead will be filled with the existing data from the iso image. The written data is laid over the existing sector: only the part of the sector the mode exposes is replaced, and the rest, such as the sync header and location, is kept as it is on the image. ECC and EDC will be recalculated on the fly for files opened in 'M2_FORM1' or 'M2_FORM2' mode, including when that mode was guessed. In any other mode, including 'M1', they are not recalculated.

The ISOReader object has the following methods:

:open(filename) -- Returns a File object off the specified file within the ISO.

This method is basically a helper over the :open() method of the Iso object, and will automatically guess the mode and size of the file.

docs.title: Calling guest code
docs.text:
PCSX.callGuest(call) runs a function of the emulated program from Lua, with arguments, and returns its result. It is meant for harnesses: feeding a decompressor deliberately broken streams, measuring how many cycles a routine takes, or checking which memory a routine writes.

It needs the interpreter, since the recompilers can't be stopped on an arbitrary address. Start with -interpreter, or turn the dynarec off in the Emulation settings and reboot. It can't be nested, which means it can't be called from a breakpoint invoker that fires during another guest call; an ExecutionFlow event listener is a fine place to call it from.

The argument is a single table:

Field Meaning pc Mandatory. The address to call, 4-byte aligned. args Table of numbers. The first four go in $a0 to $a3, the rest on the stack, following the o32 convention with its 16-byte argument save area. sp Stack pointer before the argument frame is reserved, 8-byte aligned. Defaults to the top of RAM, minus 16. The callee gets sp lowered by the frame, which is 16 bytes, or 4 bytes per argument if that is more: with the default, $sp is 0x801fffe0 on entry to a function of the 2MB RAM. The frame must be in RAM or the scratchpad if there are more than four arguments. gp If present, loaded into $gp. ra Sentinel return address, 4-byte aligned, defaults to 0x8f000000. The call ends when the program counter reaches it, so it should be somewhere the callee never legitimately jumps to. cycles Cycle budget, defaults to 100000000. stage Array of { addr = ..., data = '...' }. The strings are copied into RAM before the call, bypassing the guest's cache isolation state. fetch Array of { addr = ..., size = ... }. The ranges are read out of RAM after the call, before any rollback. isolate false (default), true or 'full', or 'ram'. See below. dirty Boolean. Report which 64kB pages of RAM the callee changed.

In every mode, the general purpose registers, the coprocessor 0 and 2 registers, the program counter and the cycle counter come back as they were. What differs is the rest of the machine:

  • isolate = false: whatever the callee did to memory stays.
  • isolate = 'ram': RAM and the scratchpad are rolled back, along with the staged inputs and the stack arguments. It is cheaper than 'full', and blind to anything that isn't RAM, which nonRamAccesses in the result tells you about.
  • isolate = true or 'full': the whole machine is rolled back, through a savestate taken before the inputs go in.

The function returns a table:

Field Meaning status 'returned' when the program counter reached ra, 'cycles' when the budget ran out, 'exception' when the callee raised one, 'unknown' otherwise. v0, v1 The values of $v0 and $v1 when the call ended. cycles Cycles spent. out The strings read by fetch, in order. dirty Addresses of the changed 64kB pages (0x80000000 or'd with the page offset), when isolate = 'ram' or dirty was requested. nonRamAccesses How many bus accesses outside of RAM happened. Zero means the callee touched nothing but RAM, so 'ram' isolation was sound for it. depth Change in the depth of the call stack monitor. A leaf function never opens a frame, so it stays 0; non-zero after a clean return means the callee unwound badly. storesDropped True when the RAM write LUT is empty, which is the case while the caches are isolated, including on a cold boot: every guest store then vanishes. Worth checking before trusting dirty, and the arguments past the fourth, which are stored through the same bus, are dropped as well. stage isn't affected. pc Only with status 'cycles': where it stopped. exceptionCode, epc, badVAddr Only with status 'exception'.

An invalid argument, an unaligned address, a stage or fetch running off the end of RAM, or a missing interpreter raises a Lua error before anything is modified.

-- Call a decompressor at 0x80012340 on a staged buffer, and read the result back.
local r = PCSX.callGuest {
    pc = 0x80012340,
    args = { 0x80100000, 0x80200000 },
    stage = { { addr = 0x80100000, data = compressed } },
    fetch = { { addr = 0x80200000, size = 0x800 } },
    isolate = 'ram',
    cycles = 5000000,
}
if r.status == 'returned' and r.nonRamAccesses == 0 then
    print(('v0 = %08x in %d cycles'):format(r.v0, r.cycles))
    print(#r.out[1], 'bytes read back,', #r.dirty, 'pages touched')
end

docs.title: Plots
docs.text:
The global implot table binds ImPlot, the plotting library that sits on top of ImGui. Like imgui, it can only be used inside the ImGui context, for instance from DrawImguiFrame. The ImPlot API is documented in its header; this page describes how the Lua binding differs from it.

local ffi = require 'ffi'
local mem = PCSX.getMemPtr()

function DrawImguiFrame()
    if imgui.Begin('RAM plot') then
        implot.safe.BeginPlot('bytes', -1, 250, function()
            implot.SetupAxes('offset', 'value')
            implot.SetupAxesLimits(0, 256, 0, 255)
            implot.PlotLine('ram', mem + 0x1000, 256)
        end)
    end
    imgui.End()
end

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Names follow ImPlot, without the ImPlot prefix: implot.BeginPlot, implot.SetupAxis, implot.PlotLine, and so on. Enumerations are in implot.constant, grouped by their ImPlot type: implot.constant.Axis.X1, implot.constant.Flags.NoTitle, implot.constant.Marker.Circle, implot.constant.Cond, implot.constant.Colormap, and so on. Run pprint(implot.constant) for the list. implot.AUTO is IMPLOT_AUTO.
  • Every Begin whose End is only required when it returned true has a counterpart in implot.safe, which takes the body as its last argument and pairs the calls, even if the body raises an error: BeginPlot, BeginSubplots, BeginAlignedPlots, BeginLegendPopup, and the BeginDragDrop* family. Prefer these.
  • ImPlot assertions are raised as Lua errors, located at the caller.
  • Data arguments are either Lua tables of numbers, which are copied, or FFI arrays and pointers of a supported scalar type, which are read in place. The latter is what makes plotting live memory above possible. All the data arguments of a call have to share the same element type, and count is required as soon as one of them is FFI data. With tables only, count defaults to the length of the shortest.
  • ImPlot overloads which only differ by arity are resolved by the shape of the arguments: when the argument after the first data array is a number or nil, it's the values form, PlotLine(label, values, count, ...). When it's an array, it's the xs/ys form, PlotLine(label, xs, ys, count, ...). The comments above each function in src/gui/implotffi.lua list the accepted forms.
  • Colors are tables with r, g, b, a fields, from 0 to 1. A nil color is the automatic one.
  • Functions with output pointers return their results instead: implot.DragLineX(id, x, ...) returns changed, x, clicked, hovered, held.
  • The trailing spec argument of the plot functions is a table of ImPlotSpec fields, LineColor, LineWeight, FillColor, FillAlpha, Marker, MarkerSize, MarkerLineColor, MarkerFillColor, Size, Offset, Stride, Flags, and the per-point arrays LineColors, FillColors, MarkerLineColors, MarkerFillColors, MarkerSizes. An unknown field is an error. implot.Spec(table) builds the cdata once for reuse.
implot.PlotScatter('points', xs, ys, #xs, {
    Marker = implot.constant.Marker.Circle,
    MarkerSize = 4,
    MarkerFillColor = { r = 1, g = 0.4, b = 0, a = 1 },
})

docs.text:

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: PCSX-Redux features a Lua API that is available through either a direct Lua console, or a Lua editor, both available through the Debug menu. The Lua VM runs on the main thread, the same one as the UI and the emulated MIPS CPU. As a result, care must be taken to not stall for too long, or the UI will become unresponsive. Using coroutines to handle long-running tasks is recommended, yielding periodically to let the UI perform some work too. The UI is probably going to run at 60FPS or so, which gives a ballpark of 15ms per frame.

docs.title: Lua engine
docs.text: The Lua engine that's being used is LuaJIT 2.1 compiled in Lua 5.2 compatibility mode. The Lua 5.1 user manual and LuaJIT user manual are recommended reads. In particular, the bindings heavily make use of LuaJIT's FFI capabilities, which allows for direct memory access within the emulator's process. This means there is little protection against dramatic crashes the LuaJIT FFI engine can cause into the emulator's process, and the user must pay extra attention while manipulating FFI objects. Despite that, the code tries as much as possible to sandbox what the Lua code does, and will prevent crashes on any recoverable exception, including OpenGL and ImGui exceptions.

docs.title: Lua console
docs.text: All of the messages coming from Lua should display into the Lua console directly. The input text there is a single line execution, so the user can type one-liner Lua statements and get an immediate result.

docs.title: Lua editor
docs.text:
The editor allows for more complex, multi-line statements to be written, such as complete functions. The editor will by default auto save its contents on the disc under the filename pcsx.lua, which can potentially be a problem if the last statement typed crashed the emulator, as it'll be reloaded on the next startup. It might become necessary to either edit the file externally, or simply delete it to recover from this state.

The auto-execution of the editor permits for rapid development loop, with immediate feedback of what's done.

For complex projects however, it is recommended to split your work into sub-modules, and use the loadfile function to load them in your main code. This implies working on your project using an external editor.

docs.title: Introduction & Rationale
docs.text:
The Iso object described in the File API page works on an existing disc image. It is not read-only, since writing to it is what drives the PPF patch system, but what it can do is patch what is already there. The builder API is the other direction: it creates a fresh ISO9660 image from scratch, with a real filesystem in it, and writes it out to any File object.

The builder is filesystem-aware. You describe the directory tree you want, attach a File object as the content of each file, and the builder computes the whole layout at the end: the primary volume descriptor, both path tables, the directory extents, the LBA of every file, and the EDC/ECC of every sector. You never compute a sector address yourself unless you specifically want to.

Everything is deferred. createRoot, createDir and createFile only build an in-memory tree, and no byte is written until close() is called. This means the order in which you declare files does not have to match the order they end up on the disc, and it means a file's LBA is not known until after close().

docs.title: Creating a builder
docs.text:
PCSX.isoBuilder(file) -- returns an ISOBuilder object

The file argument is a File object opened for writing, which will receive the image. It can be a normal file on disk, or an in-memory buffer created with Support.File.buffer() if you only want the image transiently.

:failed() -- returns true if the output file is unusable

docs.title: Writing the license sectors
docs.text:
:writeLicense(file) -- file is optional

The first 16 sectors of a PlayStation disc hold the license data. This is not a boot gate in the way it is often described: the license data is the boot logo, so what it mostly determines is what the console displays on the way in.

The file argument is a File object holding that data. It can be the official license file from the SDK, or simply a disc image dumped from another game, in which case the license is extracted from it. The two are told apart automatically, so you don't have to declare which one you are handing over.

Whether the license matters for booting depends on the machine:

  • Japanese consoles refuse to boot a disc without a Japanese license.
  • Very late European models refuse to boot a disc without a European license.
  • Every other model boots regardless, though a missing or custom license changes the logo that comes up.
  • Some emulators, unlike the hardware, refuse to boot without one at all.

A Japanese license is therefore the pragmatic choice, since it covers the widest range of consoles.

Calling writeLicense() with no argument, or with a file that failed to open, writes 16 sectors of zeroes instead. That is fine for development and for PCSX-Redux itself. No license data ships with PCSX-Redux, so you have to supply your own.

If you intend to write license sectors at all, do it before building the tree.

docs.title: The volume descriptor
docs.text:
The PVD fields that identify the volume are settable, and are padded with spaces to their fixed ISO9660 widths for you:

:setSystemIdent(str)          :getSystemIdent()
:setVolumeIdent(str)          :getVolumeIdent()
:setVolSetIdent(str)          :getVolSetIdent()
:setPublisherIdent(str)       :getPublisherIdent()
:setDataPreparerIdent(str)    :getDataPreparerIdent()
:setApplicationIdent(str)     :getApplicationIdent()
:setCopyrightFileIdent(str)   :getCopyrightFileIdent()
:setAbstractFileIdent(str)    :getAbstractFileIdent()
:setBibliographicFileIdent(str) :getBibliographicFileIdent()

The getters return the stored string with its padding trimmed off.

For a disc meant to look like a retail PlayStation release, the system identifier is PLAYSTATION. The remaining fields are cosmetic as far as the console is concerned.

Everything else in the PVD is computed during close() and cannot be set: the volume space size, the path table sizes and locations, the root directory entry, the type code, the standard identifier, and both version fields.

docs.title: Building the tree
docs.text:
:createRoot(sectorCount)               -- sectorCount defaults to 1
:createDir(parent, name, sectorCount)  -- sectorCount defaults to 1
:createFile(parent, name, contentFile)

All three return a DirTree node. createRoot must be called before anything else can be parented, and the node it returns is the root directory.

The sectorCount argument on the two directory functions is the number of sectors reserved for that directory's own extent. One sector holds roughly thirty entries depending on name lengths, so a directory with more children than that needs a larger count. It is not grown automatically.

name is the bare name. For files, the ;1 version suffix that ISO9660 requires is appended when the directory entry is serialized, so pass SYSTEM.CNF, not SYSTEM.CNF;1. Names are not validated or case-folded for you; ISO9660 level 1 wants uppercase 8.3, and it is on you to respect that if you care about the image being maximally portable.

contentFile is any File object. Its size at close() time is the size the file gets on the disc.

createRoot marks the root as having XA attributes, which is what a PlayStation disc looks like, and both createDir and createFile inherit the XA flag and the date from their parent. So setting a date on the root propagates to everything created under it afterwards, but not to anything created before.

docs.title: DirTree nodes
docs.text:
The node returned by the three creation functions carries the per-entry knobs.

Read-only properties, meaningful after close() for the ones that depend on layout:

:getName()   :getSize()   :getLBA()   :isDir()

Navigation, all returning a node or nil:

:parent()   :firstChild()   :nextSibling()

Flags:

:isHidden()     :setHidden(bool)
:shouldSkip()   :setSkip(bool)
:hasXA()        :setXA(bool)

setHidden sets the ISO9660 hidden bit on the directory entry. The file is still fully present and readable by anything that ignores the bit.

setSkip is different and much stronger: the node still participates in the layout, so it is allocated an LBA and its content is written to the disc, but no directory entry is emitted for it. The file exists on the disc and is completely invisible to the filesystem. This is how you reproduce discs that address most of their data by hardcoded LBA and only expose a handful of real entries.

Sector mode and XA:

:setSectorMode(mode)   -- 'RAW', 'M1', 'M2_RAW', 'M2_FORM1', 'M2_FORM2'
:getSectorMode()       -- returns the node's mode, as one of the above or 'GUESS'
:getXAAttribs()        :setXAAttribs(value)
:getXAFileNum()        :setXAFileNum(value)

Files default to M2_FORM1, which is what ordinary data on a PlayStation disc uses. M2_FORM2 is for streaming data such as XA audio and STR video, where the sector carries 2324 bytes and no error correction. M2_RAW hands the builder full 2336-byte sectors including the subheader, for content that has to be reproduced byte for byte.

Dates:

:setDate(year, month, day, hour, minute, second, offset)

All seven arguments default to 0 if omitted. year is an offset from 1900 and offset is the timezone in 15-minute steps, matching the ISO9660 directory record format.

Layout overrides:

:hasAnchorLBA()      :getAnchorLBA()      :setAnchorLBA(lba)      :clearAnchorLBA()
:hasDeclaredSize()   :getDeclaredSize()   :setDeclaredSize(bytes) :clearDeclaredSize()

setAnchorLBA pins a node to a specific absolute LBA instead of letting the layout pass place it. Sectors between the previous end of the layout and the anchor are padded with empty M2_FORM1 data. close() throws if the layout cursor has already advanced past a requested anchor, since that cannot be satisfied.

setDeclaredSize overrides the DataLength field of the directory entry independently of how much content is actually attached. The pair is what lets you reproduce a disc whose single directory entry declares an extent spanning hundreds of megabytes of data that is itself addressed by LBA. Attach a small piece of content, declare the real extent, and place the rest of the data with setSkip nodes.

docs.title: Closing
docs.text:
:close(threadCount) -- threadCount defaults to 0

This is where the work happens: the layout is computed, then the PVD, the volume descriptor set terminator, both path tables, the directory extents, the anchor padding and finally the file contents are written in that order.

EDC and ECC are computed for every sector the builder assembles itself, and the file contents are processed in parallel. threadCount is the number of worker threads to use for that; 0 means one per hardware thread. There is no way to turn the computation off, since an image with wrong EDC is not a useful image. The only exception is file content in RAW or M2_RAW mode, which already carries its own EDC and ECC and is written as supplied.

The builder does not add trailing padding past the end of the volume, and on real hardware that is a problem. The Mechacon has trouble seeking near the end of a disc: it regularly overshoots, and with nothing past the last real sector, it gets stuck there. Zero-filled sectors after the data are a landing zone that guarantees it cannot.

How many of them you need is a function of the read pattern. If the read is linear from the start of an extent and never goes near the edge of the written area, read-ahead slack is all there is to cover, and the 150 sectors exe2iso appends, two seconds of disc time, are right for a disc holding a single executable. If arbitrary seeks near the last written sector are possible, size against the overshoot instead: the authoring tool appends 9000, since an archive can be seeked into anywhere, including its own edge. Neither number is wrong; they answer different questions.

PCSX-Redux reads a truncated tail perfectly happily, so an image missing its padding passes every test you can run without a burner. Append the sectors after close(): the layout always starts at sector 16 and leaves the cursor past the end of the volume, so a loop of blank writeSector calls lands exactly where it should.

docs.title: A complete example
docs.text:
local out = Support.File.open('mydisc.bin', 'TRUNCATE')
local builder = PCSX.isoBuilder(out)

builder:writeLicense(Support.File.open('license.dat'))
builder:setSystemIdent('PLAYSTATION')
builder:setVolumeIdent('MYDISC')

local root = builder:createRoot()

local cnf = Support.File.buffer()
cnf:write('BOOT=cdrom:\\PSX.EXE;1\r\nTCB=4\r\nEVENT=10\r\nSTACK=801FFFF0\r\n')
cnf:rSeek(0)
builder:createFile(root, 'SYSTEM.CNF', cnf)

local exe = builder:createFile(root, 'PSX.EXE', Support.File.open('mygame.ps-exe'))

local data = builder:createDir(root, 'DATA')
builder:createFile(data, 'LEVEL1.BIN', Support.File.open('level1.bin'))

local movie = builder:createFile(data, 'INTRO.STR', Support.File.open('intro.str'))
movie:setSectorMode('M2_FORM2')

builder:close()
print('PSX.EXE landed at LBA ' .. exe:getLBA())
out:close()

Note that exe:getLBA() is only meaningful after close(), since nothing is placed before then.

docs.title: Reading the result back
docs.text:
The builder writes an image that the reader side can open directly, which makes round-tripping easy to verify without leaving Lua:

local buffer = Support.File.buffer()
local builder = PCSX.isoBuilder(buffer)
-- ...build...
builder:close()

buffer:rSeek(0)
local reader = PCSX.openIso(buffer):createReader()
local f = reader:open('DATA/LEVEL1.BIN;1')
print(f:size())

Note the rSeek(0) calls. A File object has separate read and write pointers, so a buffer you have just written content into still has its read pointer where you left it. The builder rewinds every content file itself before reading it during close(), so rewinding a buffer before handing it to createFile is only a precaution, but rewind the output before reopening it as an ISO.

This is exactly what the test suite in tests/lua/isobuilder.lua does.

docs.title: Writing raw sectors
docs.text:
Everything above builds a filesystem. The builder can also write individual sectors directly, with no ISO9660 structure involved at all, which is what you want for reproducing a disc that does not have a conventional filesystem, or for placing data at a fixed location alongside one that does.

:writeSector(data[, mode])            -- writes at the current cursor, returns the LBA used
:writeSectorAt(data, lba[, mode])     -- writes at an explicit LBA, returns it
:getCurrentLBA()                      -- where the cursor currently sits

data is a Lua string. A cdata pointer works too, but then the size has to be passed explicitly, since a pointer does not carry one:

:writeSector(ptr, size[, mode])
:writeSectorAt(ptr, size, lba[, mode])

mode defaults to M2_FORM1. Each mode consumes a different amount of data, and passing less than it needs is an error rather than a truncated sector:

mode bytes consumed notes M2_FORM1 2048 ordinary data; sync, header, subheader and EDC/ECC are generated M2_FORM2 2324 streaming data; EDC is generated M2_RAW 2336 subheader onwards, supplied by you; sync and header are generated RAW 2352 the complete frame, written verbatim

M1 and GUESS cannot be written and will raise an error.

All LBAs here are relative to the start of the image, matching the rest of the ISO API, so sector 0 is the first sector of the file.

writeSector advances the cursor by one. writeSectorAt moves the cursor to just past the sector it wrote, but only ever forwards: writing behind the cursor leaves it where it was, so you can go back and fill something in without losing your place.

Note that raw sector writes and the filesystem API write to the same output file, and nothing arbitrates between them. close() always lays the filesystem out starting at sector 16, immediately after the system area, regardless of where the sector cursor happens to be, and will happily overwrite sectors you placed by hand. If you want to mix the two, use setAnchorLBA to push the filesystem past the region you are writing yourself.

The most useful thing this buys you is patching the image after the layout exists. A common shape on real discs is a lookup table that maps some game-side index to the LBA of the data it needs, which is a chicken-and-egg problem while you are building: the table has to contain LBAs that nothing knows until the layout has been computed. Raw sector writes let you close that loop by going back afterwards.

local builder = PCSX.isoBuilder(out)
builder:writeLicense(license)
local root = builder:createRoot()

-- Reserve a sector for the table itself, plus the files it will point at.
local placeholder = Support.File.buffer()
placeholder:write(string.rep('\0', 2048))
placeholder:rSeek(0)
local table_ = builder:createFile(root, 'LBATABLE.BIN', placeholder)

local assets = {}
for i, name in ipairs(assetNames) do
    assets[i] = builder:createFile(root, name, Support.File.open(name))
end

-- Now the layout exists, and every node knows where it landed.
builder:close()

-- Build the real table from the computed LBAs and drop it over the placeholder.
local bit = require 'bit'
local sector = ''
for i, node in ipairs(assets) do
    local lba = node:getLBA()
    sector = sector .. string.char(bit.band(lba, 0xff), bit.band(bit.rshift(lba, 8), 0xff),
                                   bit.band(bit.rshift(lba, 16), 0xff), bit.band(bit.rshift(lba, 24), 0xff))
end
sector = sector .. string.rep('\0', 2048 - #sector)
builder:writeSectorAt(sector, table_:getLBA(), 'M2_FORM1')

The EDC/ECC of the rewritten sector is recomputed as part of the write, so the patched image stays consistent.

docs.title: Basic Lua
docs.text: The LuaJIT extensions are fully loaded, and can be used globally. The standard Lua libraries are loaded, and are usable. The require function exists, but isn't recommended as the loading of external DLLs might be difficult to properly accomplish. Loading pure Lua files is fine. The ffi table is loaded globally, there is no need to require it, but it'll work nonetheless. As a side-effect of Luv, Lua-compat-5.3 is loaded.

docs.title: Dear ImGui
docs.text: A good portion of ImGui is bound to the Lua environment, and it's possible for the Lua code to emit arbitrary widgets through ImGui. It is advised to consult the user manual of ImGui in order to properly understand how to make use of it. The list of current bindings can be found within the source code. Some usage examples will be provided within the case studies. Additional features and interaction is documented in the rendering page.

docs.title: OpenGL
docs.text: OpenGL is bound directly to the Lua API through FFI bindings, loosely inspired and adapted from LuaJIT-OpenCL. Some usage examples can be seen in the CRT-Lottes shader configuration page.

docs.title: ThorVG
docs.text: The ThorVG library is bound to the Lua API as the global tvg table, through FFI bindings of its C API, with some additional glue code. More explanation can be found in the rendering page.

docs.title: Luv
docs.text: For network access and interaction, PCSX-Redux uses libuv internally, and is exposed to the Lua API through Luv, tho its loop is tied to the main thread one, meaning it'll run only once per frame. There is another layer of network API available through the File API, which is more convenient and faster for simple tasks.

docs.title: Zlib
docs.text: The Zlib C-API is exposed through FFI bindings. There is another layer of Zlib API available through the File API, which is more convenient and faster for simple tasks.

docs.title: FFI-Reflect
docs.text: The FFI-Reflect library is loaded globally as the reflect symbol. It's able to generate reflection objects for the LuaJIT FFI module.

docs.title: PPrint
docs.text: The PPrint library is loaded globally as the pprint symbol. It's a more powerful print function than the one provided by Lua, and can be used to print tables in a more readable way.

docs.title: Lua-Protobuf
docs.text: The Lua-Protobuf library is available, but not loaded by default. All of its documented API should be usable straight with no additional work. It has been slightly modified, but nothing that should be visible to the user. There is some limited glue between its API and PCSX's.

docs.title: luafilesystem
docs.text: The luafilesystem library is loaded globally as the lfs symbol. It's a library that provides access to the filesystem.

docs.title: LPeg
docs.text: The LPeg library is loaded globally as the lpeg symbol, which is also what require 'lpeg' returns. It's a library that provides a pattern-matching library for Lua, which can be useful to create ad-hoc arbitrary parsers.

docs.title: FFI access
docs.text:
The Lua code can access the emulated memory and registers directly through some FFI bindings:

  • PCSX.getMemPtr() will return a cdata[uint8_t*] representing up to 8MB of emulated memory. This can be written to, but careful about the emulated i-cache in case code is being written to.
  • PCSX.getParPtr() will return a cdata[uint8_t*] representing up to 512kB of the EXP1/Parallel port memory space. This can be written to.
  • PCSX.getRomPtr() will return a cdata[uint8_t*] representing up to 512kB of the BIOS memory space. This can be written to.
  • PCSX.getScratchPtr() will return a cdata[uint8_t*] representing up to 1kB for the scratchpad memory space.
  • PCSX.getRegisters() will return a structured cdata representing all the registers present in the CPU:
  • PCSX.setGPR(index, value) writes the general purpose register index, from 0 to 33 (lo and hi are 32 and 33). Unlike a store into getRegisters().GPR, it also drops a load still pending for that register. Assigning pc through getRegisters() likewise drops a branch still pending in a delay slot.
  • PCSX.getReadLUT() will return a cdata[uint8_t**] representing the read LUT for the CPU.
  • PCSX.getWriteLUT() will return a cdata[uint8_t**] representing the write LUT for the CPU.
typedef union {
    struct {
        uint32_t r0, at, v0, v1, a0, a1, a2, a3;
        uint32_t t0, t1, t2, t3, t4, t5, t6, t7;
        uint32_t s0, s1, s2, s3, s4, s5, s6, s7;
        uint32_t t8, t9, k0, k1, gp, sp, s8, ra;
        uint32_t lo, hi;
    } n;
    uint32_t r[34];
} psxGPRRegs;

typedef union {
    uint32_t r[32];
} psxCP0Regs;

typedef union {
    uint32_t r[32];
} psxCP2Data;

typedef union {
    uint32_t r[32];
} psxCP2Ctrl;

typedef struct {
    psxGPRRegs GPR;
    psxCP0Regs CP0;
    psxCP2Data CP2D;
    psxCP2Ctrl CP2C;
    uint32_t pc;
} psxRegisters;

docs.title: Safer access
docs.text:
The above methods will return direct pointers into the emulated memory, so it's easy to crash the emulator if you're not careful. The getMemoryAsFile() method is safer, but will be slower:

  • PCSX.getMemoryAsFile() will return a File object representing the full 4GB of accessible memory. All operations on this file will be translated to the emulated memory space. This is slower than the direct access methods, but safer. Any read or write operation will be clamped to the emulated memory space, and will not crash the emulator.

docs.title: Memory mapping
docs.text:
PCSX-Redux will attempt to forward reads and writes for memory not mapped in the LUTs. This is useful for debugging, but will be slower than the direct access methods.

  • UnknownMemoryRead(address, size) will be called when a read is attempted to an unmapped memory address. The function should return an 8, 16, or 32-bit value to be returned to the CPU.
  • UnknownMemoryWrite(address, size, value) will be called when a write is attempted to an unmapped memory address. The function should return true or false indicating whether the write was handled.

See Expansion carts in Lua for how to use these, together with the LUTs, to emulate a parallel port cartridge.

docs.title: Playbook: finding where a bug lives
docs.text: When a game misbehaves in the emulator, the first question is where the problem is: in the game's own code doing something unexpected, in the CPU emulation, in the GPU, or somewhere else entirely. This page goes through the tools that answer that question from Lua: breakpoints to see what the game's code is doing, and GPU dumps to take the game out of the equation altogether. It builds on the scripted session from the previous playbook, and the examples were run against Crash Bandicoot (USA) on its title menu.

docs.title: Turning the debugger on
docs.text:
Breakpoints are only evaluated when the debugger is enabled, and the ones triggered by the CPU only work with the interpreter: the dynarec doesn't check them. So any run using them needs both flags:

pcsx-redux -testmode -stdout -lua_stdout -bios scph5501.bin -iso "Crash Bandicoot (USA).cue" -run -debugger -interpreter -dofile debug.lua

The interpreter is a lot slower than the dynarec, but a scripted session doesn't care, since its schedule is counted in emulated frames.

docs.title: Who writes this variable?
docs.text:
Diffing two RAM dumps, as shown in the previous playbook, gives candidate addresses. On Crash's title menu, the word at 0x800549f0 goes up by one on every frame. The next question is which code writes it, and a write breakpoint answers it. Here it's set from the vsync listener once the game has reached the menu, so that it doesn't fire during boot:

local frame = 0
vsyncListener = PCSX.Events.createEventListener('GPU::Vsync', function()
    frame = frame + 1
    if frame == 3600 then
        writerBp = PCSX.addBreakpoint(0x800549f0, 'Write', 4, 'who writes the counter', function(address, width)
            local r = PCSX.getRegisters()
            print(string.format('write to %08x (%d bytes) by pc=%08x ra=%08x', address, width, r.pc, r.GPR.n.ra))
            return false
        end)
    end
end)

Which prints:

write to 800549f0 (4 bytes) by pc=8003eed8 ra=8004b844

pc is the store instruction, and ra usually points back into the function's caller, which is the next place to look in the assembly view or in a disassembler. Returning false from the callback removes the breakpoint after its first hit; returning true keeps it, and the callback then runs on every write. The callback doesn't pause the emulator unless it calls PCSX.pauseEmulator() itself, so a script keeps running through the hits.

docs.title: What is it asking the BIOS?
docs.text:
Games call the BIOS through three entry points, at 0xa0, 0xb0 and 0xc0, with the function number in register t1. Execution breakpoints on these three addresses log every BIOS call, along with who made it and its first arguments:

local kernelBps = {}

local function logKernelCalls()
    for _, entry in ipairs({ 0xa0, 0xb0, 0xc0 }) do
        kernelBps[#kernelBps + 1] = PCSX.addBreakpoint(entry, 'Exec', 4, 'kernel call', function()
            local r = PCSX.getRegisters().GPR.n
            print(string.format('%02X(%02x) from %08x a0=%08x a1=%08x', entry, bit.band(r.t1, 0xff), r.ra, r.a0, r.a1))
            return true
        end)
    end
end

local function stopKernelCalls()
    for _, bp in ipairs(kernelBps) do bp:remove() end
    kernelBps = {}
end

Calling logKernelCalls() at frame 3500 and stopKernelCalls() ten frames later gives lines such as:

B0(17) from 8003eb2c a0=00000040 a1=1f801070
A0(2a) from 80040e98 a0=80054ad8 a1=8005a49c
B0(16) from 8003e470 a0=00000000 a1=00000000

The function numbers can be looked up in the BIOS function list of psx-spx. Keep the window short, as every call prints a line.

docs.title: Following the code
docs.text:
An execution breakpoint can also cover a whole range. One spanning the 2MB of RAM fires on every instruction, which makes a trace of everything the CPU runs. It's slow, so arm it at the point of interest, and remove it as soon as it has seen enough:

local count = 0
traceBp = PCSX.addBreakpoint(0x80000000, 'Exec', 0x200000, 'trace', function(address)
    local r = PCSX.getRegisters()
    print(string.format('%08x ra=%08x v0=%08x', address, r.GPR.n.ra, r.GPR.n.v0))
    count = count + 1
    return count < 1000
end)

This is the tool for questions such as "which path does the code take after this write", or "what runs between this exception and the return from it".

docs.title: Taking the game out of the picture: GPU dumps
docs.text:
When the problem is on the screen, the question becomes whether the game sent the GPU the wrong commands, or whether the GPU emulation drew the right commands wrong. A GPU dump settles it. It records everything the GPU receives, starting from a snapshot of its state, so the same frames can later be replayed without the game, the CPU or the rest of the machine:

-- in the vsync listener, at the frames of interest
if frame == 3600 then PCSX.GPU.startDump('title.gpd') end
if frame == 3604 then
    PCSX.GPU.stopDump()
    print('dumped frames: ' .. PCSX.GPU.getDumpFrames())
end

The recording begins at the next vsync after startDump, so the example above records 3 complete frames. The dump can then be replayed by the dump player, which runs its own GPU, separate from the emulator's:

local player = PCSX.GPU.DumpPlayer
player.load('title.gpd')
while player.step() do end      -- one frame per step, false at the end of the dump
print('replayed up to frame ' .. player.getFrame())

local out = Support.File.open('replay.vram', 'TRUNCATE')
out:writeMoveSlice(player.getVRAM())   -- 16bpp, 1024 pixels per row
out:close()
player.unload()

PCSX.GPU.getVRAM() returns the emulator's own VRAM in the same layout. On the Crash title menu, replaying the dump gives back the displayed frame byte for byte. Other areas of VRAM, such as textures, can differ, depending on what was uploaded around the moment the dump stopped, so comparing the display area is what tells whether the replay reproduces the picture.

From there, the dump is a self-contained test case:

  • If the replay shows the problem, the GPU received commands that produce it. Replaying the same file through a build with a candidate fix, and comparing the VRAM, tells whether the fix works, without ever booting the game again.
  • If the replay looks right while the game looks wrong, the problem is elsewhere, on the CPU side or in timing.
  • The commands themselves are in the file, so the geometry the game sent can be drawn separately, to check whether it was already broken before reaching the GPU.

docs.title: A worked example
docs.text:
This is how the torn spider and web in MediEvil's graveyard (issue #2012) were tracked down. A scripted session played the game to the right frames and dumped them. Drawing the polygons from the dump as a wireframe showed intact geometry, so the game was sending correct data. Replaying the same dump in the emulator reproduced the shards, which put the problem in the GPU's command parsing. The log was also printing Got an invalid line command, and the culprit turned out to be a polyline whose very first word looked like the end-of-polyline marker. With the parsing fixed, the same dump replayed cleanly, and both the interpreter and the dynarec had torn identically before, which ruled the CPU out.

That log line is a cheap first check when geometry looks torn: any Got an invalid line command message means the emulated GPU desynchronized from the command stream, and the vertices themselves may well be fine.

docs.title: Playbook: scripting a game session
docs.text:
Most reverse engineering work ends up needing the same thing over and over: get the game to a given screen, poke at it, look at the result, and do it all again after changing something. Doing this by hand is slow, and it's never quite the same run twice. This page shows how to turn it into a script, using nothing but the Lua API, so the emulator boots the game, presses the buttons, takes the screenshots and dumps the memory by itself, on the same frames every time.

The example uses Crash Bandicoot (USA), which reaches its title menu after about 3600 frames with no input at all, but nothing here is specific to that game.

docs.title: The clock: counting vsyncs
docs.text:
A script needs a notion of time that doesn't depend on how fast the host is. The GPU::Vsync event fires once per emulated vertical blank, so counting those gives a frame number that means the same thing on every machine:

local frame = 0
vsyncListener = PCSX.Events.createEventListener('GPU::Vsync', function()
    frame = frame + 1
end)

The listener is stored in a global on purpose: if it gets garbage collected, it stops firing.

docs.title: A schedule
docs.text:
With a frame counter, the rest is a table of things to do at given frames. Here's a complete script, session.lua, which takes a screenshot and a RAM dump of the title menu, presses Start, then takes another screenshot once the game has moved on, and quits:

local outdir = os.getenv('SESSION_OUT') or '.'
local pad = PCSX.SIO0.slots[1].pads[1]
local B = PCSX.CONSTS.PAD.BUTTON

local frame = 0
local schedule = {}

local function at(f, action)
    schedule[f] = schedule[f] or {}
    table.insert(schedule[f], action)
end

-- Press a button, and release it 6 frames later. A press lasting a single
-- frame can fall between two reads of the pad by the game.
local function tap(f, button)
    at(f, function() pad.setOverride(button) end)
    at(f + 6, function() pad.clearOverride(button) end)
end

-- Save the current display as a binary PPM file, which most image tools
-- can open or convert. This handles the usual 16bpp display mode; the
-- 24bpp mode used by movies needs a different conversion.
local function shot(f, name)
    at(f, function()
        local ss = PCSX.GPU.takeScreenShot()
        local w, h = ss.width, ss.height
        if ss.data.size ~= w * h * 2 then
            print('shot ' .. name .. ': not a 16bpp display, skipped')
            return
        end
        -- 5 bits per component, red in the low bits.
        local p = ffi.cast('const uint16_t*', ss.data.data)
        local px = {}
        for i = 0, w * h - 1 do
            local c = p[i]
            local r = bit.band(c, 31) * 8
            local g = bit.band(bit.rshift(c, 5), 31) * 8
            local b = bit.band(bit.rshift(c, 10), 31) * 8
            px[#px + 1] = string.char(r, g, b)
        end
        local f = io.open(outdir .. '/' .. name .. '.ppm', 'wb')
        f:write(string.format('P6\n%d %d\n255\n', w, h))
        f:write(table.concat(px))
        f:close()
        print(string.format('shot %s %dx%d at frame %d', name, w, h, frame))
    end)
end

-- Write the 2MB of main RAM to a file.
local function dumpRAM(f, name)
    at(f, function()
        local f = io.open(outdir .. '/' .. name .. '.bin', 'wb')
        f:write(ffi.string(PCSX.getMemPtr(), 0x200000))
        f:close()
        print(string.format('ram %s at frame %d', name, frame))
    end)
end

shot(3600, 'title')
dumpRAM(3600, 'title')
tap(3700, B.START)
shot(4300, 'after-start')
at(4310, function() PCSX.quit(0) end)

vsyncListener = PCSX.Events.createEventListener('GPU::Vsync', function()
    frame = frame + 1
    local actions = schedule[frame]
    if actions then
        for _, action in ipairs(actions) do action() end
    end
end)

A few notes about the pieces:

  • The screenshot is the display area as the GPU sees it, so its width is the one the game programmed (512 pixels here), without any aspect ratio correction. See the GPU section for the structure it returns.
  • setOverride holds a button down until clearOverride releases it, regardless of what the keyboard or a gamepad are doing. The button names are in PCSX.CONSTS.PAD.BUTTON, see Pads.
  • The RAM dump is a plain 2MB file, where offset n is address 0x80000000 + n. Two of them taken a few frames apart are the cheapest way to find a variable: diff them, and look for the words that changed the way you expect. For instance, a word that goes up by exactly one on every frame is a frame counter.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
The script is loaded with -dofile, and the run is made independent from your own settings with -testmode, which neither loads nor saves them:

pcsx-redux -testmode -stdout -lua_stdout -bios scph5501.bin -iso "Crash Bandicoot (USA).cue" -run -dofile session.lua

-stdout and -lua_stdout send the logs and the output of print to the terminal, which is where the shot and ram lines above end up. Passing -bios explicitly is a good habit for scripted runs, so they don't depend on whichever BIOS the settings happen to point at.

On a machine without a display, such as a build server, the same command runs under a virtual X server:

xvfb-run -a pcsx-redux -testmode -stdout -lua_stdout -bios scph5501.bin -iso "Crash Bandicoot (USA).cue" -run -dofile session.lua

Since the schedule is keyed to emulated frames, the same build, BIOS and command line give the same frames on every run: two runs of a script like this one produce byte-identical RAM dumps at frame 3600. This is what makes a script a good regression test: once a screenshot shows the problem at frame N, it shows it at frame N every time, and a fix can be checked the same way.

docs.title: Savestates
docs.text:
Booting the game every time is fine when the interesting part is near the start. When it's an hour in, play there once, save a state, and start the script from it instead:

local state = PCSX.createSaveState()        -- a Slice holding the state
-- ...
PCSX.loadSaveState(state)

A state can also be written to a file and loaded back in a later run:

local out = Support.File.open('/path/to/level3.state', 'TRUNCATE')
